extracted.intended_audience: general educated public / readers of Popular Science Monthly (late 19th-century popular-science readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, late-19th-century popular-science magazine columns on technology, natural history, hygiene, and social practices aimed at informing and advising a general readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typography and lighting to protect readers' eyesight
rubrics_metrics.description: Best positions and best lights, clear type, plain inks, with the best paper of yellowish tints, and abundant space between the lines, afford the best safeguards against harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers who work by poor light risk injuring their eyesight; many who use eyes constantly (engravers, watchmakers) take special precautions. The physical labour of reading is large (example: a 500-page book with 40 lines/page and 50 letters/line contains ~1,000,000 letters). To reduce harm: use optimal reading positions and artificial lighting, clear and plain type, yellowish-tinted paper, and increased line spacing. Anti-patterns: departures from common type that make matter harder to take in; poor/insufficient lighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luminous paint — physical and optical performance criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Luminous paint must absorb light rays and subsequently emit them at increased wavelength; maximum excitation comes from violet and ultra-violet rays, while red and yellow rays diminish long-term luminosity (via calorific effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance notes and examples: short exposure to ordinary daylight can produce a high degree of illumination; intense sun or burning magnesium may cause initial brightening followed by faster early loss but slow subsequent fading; a specimen sealed in 1764 still glowed (historical example). Sensitivity demonstration: electric sparks or a lucifer-match can impress images on previously dark-kept painted cards. Practical implication: prefer excitation sources rich in violet/UV for charging. Anti-patterns: continuous exposure to red/yellow (heat) will reduce long-term glow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luminous paint — durability, coverage, cost, and application suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess luminous paint by durability against weather and sea-water, duration of afterglow, coverage per unit, cost per unit, and suitability for intended applications (clocks, match-boxes, railway roofs, buoys, life-buoys, diver clothing, powder-magazines, coal-mines, ship-to-ship signaling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturer data cited: durable against weather and sea-water; one pound will paint ~28 square feet; cost reported ~28 shillings (~$7) per pound (previously higher), with expectation of further price reduction potentially below white-lead cost. Functional uses prioritized where persistent low-level light is valuable or where open flame is hazardous (e.g., powder-magazines, coal-mines). Example performance: after moderate daylight exposure for two hours, a card was visible enough to read a watch dial after 26 hours in total darkness. Commercial viability metrics: cost per pound, coverage, and durability relative to existing materials. Anti-patterns: assuming all light sources are equally effective; not accounting for heat-induced rapid decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for an electric lighting system (Jablochkoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key metrics for assessing the Jablochkoff electric-light system: operational reliability (hours of continuous nightly operation), scalability/ability to extend system without disrupting daily efficiency, cost per light per hour (contract price changes), and versatility of deployment across different environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational history: system maintained regularly for six hours each night since first installation; extensions were added without interfering with apparatus efficiency. Cost trajectory given (examples of reductions over contract extensions: originally Gd. per light per hour; later reduced to 5 d., then 3 d., and on renewal to 2½ d. per light per hour). Versatility: deployed on streets, bridges, railway-stations, theatres, circuses, docks, ships, hotels, private residences, etc.; geographically widespread (1,716 lights in various countries, 198 in England at time of report). Scoring/decision factors: reliability under continuous nightly use, cost trend and current price per light-hour, maintainability when scaling, and proven performance across multiple site types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and practical justification criterion for vivisection
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivisection should be judged by its practical results — specifically whether it yields means of curing human disease or assuaging human pain; animal experiments are justified when they produce knowledge that protects or saves human life or that cannot be obtained otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Richet's stated standard: if vivisection leads to cures or effective treatments, it is lawful. Supporting examples cited: discovery of circulation (Galen, Harvey), transfusion, knowledge of inhalation poisoning and prevention, quantitative hygiene (air requirements), gastric digestion studies (artificial fistulas), nutrition via controlled alimentation experiments, nerve and paralysis treatment insights, galvanization therapy, sympathetic ophthalmia treatment, cataract treatment, bone regeneration and grafting research, vasomotor theory, and safety testing of new medicines and poisons on animals before human trials. Operational implication: necessity and practical human benefit are the primary ethical metrics; anti-pattern: forbidding animal experiments to the extent that risky human testing would be required instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural specifications and target outcomes for foot binding (compression of Chinese women's feet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Described procedural parameters for foot-binding: timing (begun after child learns to walk), bandage dimensions (about two inches wide and two yards long for first year; five yards for subsequent years), wrapping technique, and target anatomical outcome (indentation ~1.5 inches from the ground to the instep; toes drawn over the sole so only the ball of the great-toe touches the ground).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise method: lay end of strip on instep inside, carry over toes and under foot drawing four toes down onto sole, pass over foot and around heel, repeat with successive layers until strip used and sewn tightly; use powdered alum to prevent ulceration and odor; monthly soaking in hot water and careful unwinding to abrade dead cuticle; expect frequent ulcers, sloughing of flesh, occasional loss of toes; cultural valuation: smaller, more delicate feet prized despite severe damage. These are prescriptive measurements and process details that define the intended 'successful' outcome; anti-patterns: premature or improper binding leading to uncontrolled infection or loss beyond cultural expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative criteria for identifying causes of sea and lake water coloration
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine why water is colored (red, green, etc.), investigators should sample the water and examine it microscopically to identify minute algae, oscillatoria, diatoms, crustaceans, infusoria, eggs, bacteria, or spores; correlate observations with geography, temperature, season, and species distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance: Ehrenberg and Dupont identified thread-like dark-red oscillatoria in the Red Sea by microscopic sampling; Darwin observed similar plants near Abrolhos Islands; diatoms may form large 'sawdust sea' mats and are linked to seasonal color changes (green in warmer months, blue in colder); some colorings caused by animal plankton or bacteria (can be irritating to skin); red deposits on decaying seaweeds may be bacterial. Investigative factors: species identification, extent of coverage (miles), relation to temperature/season, geographic distribution, and known ecological effects (e.g., fish kills). Anti-patterns: assuming blood or supernatural causes (e.g., 'bloody rain') without microscopic/biological analysis.
